phonemes.desc: Long omega [ɔː], the stressed first syllable that opens the name of dreams.
Diphthong [ei̯], the middle syllable that gives the name its rising sound.
Short [r] plus [o] plus [s], the agent-noun ending: "the dreamer" or "the dream itself".

pronunciation.approximation: 'oh-NEH-ros' — stress on the first syllable, the middle vowel gliding like the 'ay' in 'say,' and a clean final '-ros'.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: Ὄνειρος (Oneiros), singular; Οἰνείρων or Ὄνειροι in the plural

kin.label: Etymology
kin.form: Uncertain; possibly from a root meaning "to say" or "to see" in sleep

kin.label: Latin
kin.form: Somnus for sleep itself; the Oneiroi appear in Latin as the sons of Somnus in Ovid

pronunciation.note: Óneiros is Tier 1 because the Greek Ὄνειρος carries length (omega) and the acute accent on the first syllable, features the ASCII form oneiros flattens.

domains.title: The Dream
domains.subtitle: Personification of Dreams and Dream-Visions
domains.lead: Óneiros is the Greek personification of the dream: the winged figure or figures who pass through the gates of horn and ivory, carrying true messages or false delusions to sleeping mortals. He is one of the many children of Nýx, Night, and in Homer he serves the gods as a messenger who takes human shape in sleep.

cards.name: Son of Night
cards.desc: Hesiod makes Óneiros one of the children of Nýx, born without a father in the dark before the gods.

cards.name: Messenger Through Sleep
cards.desc: In the Odyssey, a dream takes the form of a woman to stand beside Penelope's bed and speak to her.

cards.name: The Gate of Dreams
cards.desc: In the Odyssey, dreams pass through gates of horn (true) and ivory (false), an image of sleep's ambiguity.

cards.name: False and True Dreams
cards.desc: Some dreams are winged with truth, others with deception; Óneiros carries both kinds.

symbols.name: Wings
symbols.meaning: The speed with which dreams cross from the realm of sleep to the sleeper

symbols.name: Mist or cloud
symbols.meaning: The insubstantial, shifting nature of dream-visions

symbols.name: The gates of horn and ivory
symbols.meaning: The two paths by which true and false dreams reach mortals

symbols.name: Stars or night sky
symbols.meaning: The darkness from which dreams descend, children of Nýx

mythology.lead: Óneiros moves through Greek literature as a servant of the gods, a child of Night, and the ambiguous voice that speaks to sleepers.

myths.title: Children of Night
myths.text: Hesiod lists Óneiros among the children of Nýx, born without a father: "And Nýx bore hateful Moîra and black Kēr, and Thanatos and Hypnos, and the tribe of Oneiroi." The Oneiroi are therefore siblings of death and sleep, related to fate and the dark. They are not gods of cult but powers of the night.

myths.title: The Gates of Horn and Ivory
myths.text: Penelope, troubled by dreams, asks a dream-visitor about their truth. The dream explains that there are two gates of dreams: one of horn, through which true dreams pass, and one of ivory, through which deceptive ones come. The image gives Greek literature one of its most enduring metaphors for the ambiguity of sleep.

myths.title: Dream Messenger of Zeús
myths.text: At the opening of the Iliad's second book, Zeús sends a dream to Agamemnon to lure him into battle. The dream takes the form of Nestor and stands at the king's head, speaking with a voice like the old counselor's. The scene establishes the Oneiroi as divine messengers who can wear the shape of the living.

myths.title: The Cave of Sleep
myths.text: Ovid gives the Oneiroi a Latin home in the cave of Somnus, where a thousand dreams lie waiting to be sent. Among them is Morpheus, the shape-shifter, who becomes the most famous of the dream-figures in later Western art. The Roman tradition separates and renames the dream-powers, but the Greek Óneiros remains their source.

lore.syncretism: The Greek Oneiroi were absorbed into Roman poetry as the children of Somnus, and Ovid's Morpheus, Phobetor, and Phantasos became the standard dream-figures of European literature. In the Near East, dream-gods and dream-demons had long served as messengers of the divine, and the Greek figure may have been shaped by contact with Mesopotamian and Egyptian oneirocritic traditions. Within Greek religion, dreams were often interpreted as communications from gods or the dead, and incubation sanctuaries — especially of Asklepios — specialized in healing dreams. Óneiros is the personification of that whole ambiguous commerce between sleepers and the divine.
lore.culturalLegacy: Óneiros survives in the English word "oneiric" and in every discussion of dreams as prophecy, psychology, or art. Freud and Jung made the interpretation of dreams central to modern psychology; the Greek figure remains the mythic name for the dream as messenger. In literature, the gates of horn and ivory have been reused from Virgil to Chaucer to modern fantasy. Restoring Óneiros preserves the Greek length and accent that announce the dream as a power, not merely a private experience.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Óneiros is the voice that speaks when the will is asleep. He is not a god of temples but a power of the night, a child of Nýx who carries messages we cannot receive by daylight. Some of those messages are true and some are false, and the dreamer must learn to tell them apart.

To meditate on Óneiros is to meditate on the part of the mind that thinks without asking permission. Dreams show us what we know before we know it; they also deceive us with what we most want to believe. The restoration of his name is a small recognition that the night has its own intelligences, and that they deserve their original voice.

lore.archaeology: Óneiros is a literary and iconographic figure rather than a cult deity. Votive reliefs and vase-paintings sometimes show Hypnos (Sleep) and Thanatos (Death) with wings, and the dream as a small winged figure. The major material context is not a temple but the incubation sanctuaries of Asklepios, where sleepers sought healing dreams. The Greek oneirocritic tradition is preserved in papyri and Byzantine dream-manuals descended from older Near Eastern collections.
